👔 The Priestly Garments Atone — reconciling atonement-by-vestment with punishment-by-leprosy

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Speech, Atonement, and Rebuke
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 16a–16b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing yesterday's discussion of malicious speech, the daf opens with practical guidance on when repeating information does not count as lashon hara, and warns that even public praise can curdle into harm. Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani then lists seven sins that bring leprous marks — malicious speech among them — each proven from a biblical episode, from Joab's house to King Uzziah. Rabbi Anani bar Sason's teaching that the High Priest's garments atone for these same sins seems to contradict the leprosy list, and the Gemara works out how both can be true, alongside a further view that bloodshed and malicious speech alone are atoned outside the normal sacrificial system entirely. The daf then turns to the mitzva of rebuke — how insistently one must correct another, and where that obligation ends — before closing with rulings on how long a guest should tolerate poor treatment and just how minor a hardship still counts as genuine suffering.

slides.title: 🩹 Seven Sins That Bring Leprous Marks
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani's list, each proven from a biblical episode

steps.content: 1️⃣ Malicious speech — 'whoever defames his neighbor in secret, I will destroy him' (Psalms 101:5)
2️⃣ Bloodshed — Joab's house is cursed with leprosy for the murder of Avner (II Samuel 3:29)
3️⃣ A vain oath — Gehazi is struck with leprosy after inducing Naaman to swear falsely
4️⃣ Forbidden relations — Pharaoh's household is afflicted over Sarai (Genesis 12:17)
5️⃣ Arrogance — King Uzziah is struck with leprosy after his prideful act in the Temple
6️⃣ Theft — the leprous house is emptied first: 'he gathered what wasn't his; let the priest scatter his property'
7️⃣ Stinginess — the verse calls him 'the one who owns the house,' one who hoarded it exclusively for himself

slides.title: 👔 The Priestly Garments Atone — A Contradiction?
slides.subtitle: Reconciling atonement-by-vestment with punishment-by-leprosy

lines.speaker: R' Anani b. Sason
lines.text: Each priestly garment atones for a specific sin: the tunic for bloodshed, the trousers for forbidden relations, the mitre for arrogance, the belt for wrongful thoughts, the breastplate for corrupt judgment, the ephod for idolatry — and the ROBE, with its bells, for malicious speech.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But doesn't that contradict Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani's claim that lashon hara causes LEPROSY, not atonement by a garment?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: No contradiction: if the malicious words actually caused harm or discord, leprosy still comes. If they caused no real damage, the robe atones instead.

lines.speaker: Further objection
lines.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also taught that bloodshed and malicious speech have NO atonement through ordinary offerings at all — bloodshed through the broken-necked heifer, lashon hara through the INCENSE (Numbers 17:12)!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Also reconcilable: the heifer atones when the murderer is unknown, the tunic when he is known but cannot be executed; the incense atones for PRIVATE malicious speech, the robe for PUBLIC malicious speech.

slides.title: ⚖️ How Far Must Rebuke (Tochacha) Go?
slides.subtitle: The obligation to correct another — and its outer limit

steps.content: 1️⃣ Seeing a fault in another obligates rebuking him — and rebuking again if the first attempt fails — but never to the point of humiliating him
2️⃣ Rabbi Tarfon: 'I doubt anyone in this generation can even RECEIVE rebuke' — tell someone to remove a splinter, and he answers, 'remove the beam from your own eyes'

3️⃣ Three views on the outer limit of the obligation itself: Rav — until he might be struck; Shmuel — until he might be cursed; Rabbi Yochanan — until mere reprimand, all drawn from Shaul's escalating anger at Yonatan
4️⃣ Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: complaining about Akiva to their teacher, again and again, only deepened Akiva's love for him — proving 'rebuke a wise man and he will love you'

slides.title: 🏠 A Guest's Patience, and the Measure of 'Suffering'
slides.subtitle: How much should one tolerate before reacting?

boxes.title: How Long Should a Guest Stay Despite Poor Treatment?
items: Rav: until the host actually strikes him
Shmuel: until the host packs his belongings and puts them on his back

boxes.title: What Counts as Real 'Suffering'?
items: Rabbi Elazar: a robe woven for you that simply doesn't fit right
Even smaller: wine mixed with the wrong-temperature water, or reaching for three coins and getting only two

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The school of Rabbi Yishmael: anyone who passes forty days without any suffering at all has, in effect, already received his reward in this world — a life entirely free of minor troubles is itself remarkable.

summary.principle: The Gemara treats the tongue's damage as uniquely severe yet uniquely remediable — atoned by the incense or the High Priest's robe when no real harm results, punished by leprosy when it does — and pairs this with equally exacting standards for rebuking others without humiliating them and for recognizing even minor hardship as genuine suffering.

flowSteps.content: 🗣️ Speech before three witnesses isn't malicious to repeat; public praise can boomerang into harm
🩹 Seven sins bring leprosy, malicious speech chief among them, each proven from a biblical episode

columns.content: 👔 The robe/incense atone when words cause no real harm; leprosy follows when they do
⚖️ Rebuke must persist but never humiliate; a guest's patience and 'suffering' both have defined limits

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: words and interpersonal conduct are held to a precise, textually-grounded standard — as exacting as any monetary law in the tractate

quiz.q: According to Rabba bar Rav Huna, why does information said in the presence of three people lose its status as forbidden malicious speech when repeated?
o: Because three witnesses make any statement legally true
Because it can be assumed the information will spread regardless, as 'your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend'
Because Jewish law requires three witnesses for any testimony
Because the original speaker becomes liable instead
quiz.e: The reasoning is practical: once said before three people, the information is effectively already public and will spread on its own.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, which biblical figure's household was cursed with leprosy specifically for the sin of bloodshed?
o: Pharaoh's household, over Sarai
Joab's house, for the murder of Avner
King Uzziah, for his arrogance
Gehazi, for a vain oath
quiz.e: The verse in II Samuel 3:29 curses Joab's house with affliction, including leprosy, as punishment for his murder of Avner.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile Rabbi Anani bar Sason's claim that the High Priest's robe atones for malicious speech with Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani's claim that malicious speech causes leprosy?
o: It rejects one of the two teachings entirely
If the malicious words caused actual harm, leprosy still results; if they caused no real damage, the robe atones instead
The robe only atones for men, leprosy only afflicts women
Malicious speech is redefined so the two teachings never overlap
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes based on outcome: harmful, effective malicious speech brings leprosy, while ineffective, harmless malicious speech is atoned for by the robe.

quiz.q: According to Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute, what marks the outer limit of the obligation to keep rebuking someone?
o: Rav: until struck; Shmuel: until cursed; Rabbi Yochanan: until merely reprimanded — all derived from Shaul's escalating reaction to Yonatan's rebuke
There is no limit; rebuke must continue indefinitely
The obligation ends after exactly three attempts, according to all three
The dispute concerns only who may give rebuke, not how far it goes
quiz.e: All three positions are drawn from the same verse describing King Shaul's response to his son Yonatan's rebuke over his treatment of David, each reading a different point in that escalation as the limit.

quiz.q: According to the school of Rabbi Yishmael, what is notable about someone who passes forty days without experiencing any suffering at all?
o: He is considered especially righteous and will be rewarded further
He has, in effect, already received his reward in this world, with nothing further owed in the World-to-Come
He is suspected of having sinned secretly
The teaching applies only to Torah scholars
quiz.e: The baraita teaches that a life entirely free of even minor suffering for forty days is itself remarkable, suggesting the person has already collected his due reward in this world.
